content.text: The first slice will be the report-ingress boundary: lost-pet clients can obtain the same constrained private upload grant used for found pets, finalize an optional image with the report, persist only the finalized object name, and publish contact-redacted payload v4. The decoder and notification path will continue accepting raw/v1, v2, and v3. Asynchronous analysis and matcher deferral remain separate follow-up PRs, so this slice is deployable and rollback-safe on its own.

content.text:
## Recommendation

Use **Google Cloud Identity Platform** for PetSpotR’s human users.

Keep the existing **Google Cloud IAM/service-account OIDC** for Pub/Sub and service-to-service authentication. Optionally add **Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)** later if the operator console becomes a separate internal application.

This fits PetSpotR better than Auth0, Clerk, or self-hosted Keycloak because the application already runs on Cloud Run, Firestore, GCS, and Google-managed OIDC.

Importantly, Identity Platform should authenticate people; it should not decide whether someone owns a report.

```text
Browser
  │ Identity Platform login
  ▼
PetSpotR session endpoint
  │ Secure HttpOnly session cookie
  ▼
Go authentication middleware
  │ Principal: issuer + subject + verified email
  ▼
PetSpotR authorization
  ├── report ownership in private Firestore state
  ├── shelter membership in Firestore
  ├── coarse operator role
  └── immutable audit records

Pub/Sub / service calls
  └── existing Google service-account OIDC
```

This directly supports the missing boundary documented in [docs/DEVELOPMENT.md](/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/petspotr/docs/DEVELOPMENT.md:474).

## Comparison

| Platform | Main advantages | Main disadvantages | PetSpotR fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Google Identity Platform** | Native GCP administration and billing; Go Admin SDK; browser SDK; email/social/phone authentication; MFA, OIDC, SAML, and multi-tenancy; local Auth emulator; inexpensive consumer tier | Firebase-branded SDKs; provider-specific session/token APIs; fine-grained authorization remains our responsibility; enterprise federation has a separate, higher MAU price | **Best overall** |
| **Auth0** | Very mature customer identity product; polished hosted login; strong Actions/extensibility, organizations, RBAC, attack protection, passkeys and enterprise federation | More expensive once paid capabilities and organizations are needed; many useful controls are plan-gated; another vendor/control plane; more configuration than PetSpotR currently needs | Best if enterprise shelter federation becomes the dominant requirement |
| **Clerk** | Excellent ready-made authentication UI; fast frontend integration; Go SDK; strong user and organization management | Optimized around component-oriented frontend stacks; less natural for PetSpotR’s server-rendered Go application; MFA and richer production controls require paid plans; substantial UI/session coupling | Best for speed of frontend implementation, not architectural fit |
| **Keycloak** | Open source; OIDC/OAuth/SAML; full data and deployment control; social login, federation, roles, policies, and customization | We would own credential-system uptime, database, TLS, patching, upgrades, backups, key rotation, monitoring, abuse protection and incident response | Too much operational burden today |
| **IAP** | Excellent Google-managed authentication and IAM enforcement in front of an internal Cloud Run application | IAM-oriented access is awkward for public owners and finders; not a complete consumer sign-up/account system | Use only for a separate operator/admin application |

### Google Identity Platform: specific strengths

- The free Tier 1 allowance currently covers the first **50,000 MAU** for email, phone, anonymous, and social authentication. Beyond that, pricing is published per MAU. Enterprise OIDC/SAML connections are billed separately and become chargeable after 50 MAU per project. [Identity Platform pricing](https://cloud.google.com/identity-platform/pricing)
- It provides email and social login plus MFA, OIDC, SAML, blocking functions and multi-tenancy, with a 99.95% SLA. Its client SDKs retain Firebase naming for backward compatibility. [Google’s product comparison](https://docs.cloud.google.com/identity-platform/docs/product-comparison)
- The Go Admin SDK supports ID-token verification, user management and custom claims, fitting the existing Go services. [Admin SDK documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/identity-platform/docs/install-admin-sdk)
- It supports server-created session cookies with configurable lifetimes, revocation checks, and secure `HttpOnly` cookie policies. Google explicitly calls out CSRF protection for the token-to-session exchange. [Session-cookie guidance](https://firebase.google.com/docs/auth/admin/manage-cookies)
- The Authentication emulator supports browser flows, ID-token verification and session cookies, fitting PetSpotR’s existing emulator-heavy TDD workflow. [Authentication emulator](https://firebase.google.com/docs/emulator-suite/connect_auth)
- Users and password hashes can be exported/imported, which reduces—but does not eliminate—migration lock-in. [User migration documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/identity-platform/docs/migrating-users)

### Its important limitations

- Identity Platform roles are not a replacement for domain authorization. Custom claims are limited to 1,000 bytes, propagate on token refresh, and are explicitly not intended for profile or application data. [Custom-claims guidance](https://firebase.google.com/docs/auth/admin/custom-claims)
- Shelter membership, report ownership, match access and lifecycle permissions should therefore remain in Firestore.
- Revocation checking can add a provider request during session verification. We should use it deliberately for sensitive actions rather than blindly adding that latency everywhere.
- SMS authentication and SMS MFA introduce both direct cost and abuse exposure. I would begin with Google sign-in plus verified email authentication and defer phone authentication.
- I would not initially model shelters as Identity Platform tenants. A user may interact personally and as a member of one or more shelters; PetSpotR’s own membership records model that more naturally.

## Why Auth0 is the strongest alternative

Auth0 becomes preferable if PetSpotR soon needs many shelter-specific SAML/OIDC connections, self-service enterprise SSO, extensive login-time workflows, advanced attack protection, or contractual enterprise support.

Its current free plan covers up to 25,000 MAU, while paid plans add MFA, per-organization RBAC, audit-log streaming and larger operational limits. Some capabilities remain restricted by plan and organization count, with Enterprise carrying the 99.99% SLA. [Auth0 pricing and plan comparison](https://auth0.com/pricing)

That is a richer enterprise CIAM offering, but PetSpotR would be paying for flexibility it does not presently need.

## Why not Clerk or Keycloak

Clerk is attractive if our top priority is shipping a polished login/profile UI with minimal frontend work. Its current free tier covers 50,000 monthly retained users, while paid tiers add MFA, custom session lifetimes, longer logs and advanced B2B features. [Clerk pricing](https://clerk.com/pricing) The trade-off is tighter coupling to Clerk’s frontend and session model without improving PetSpotR’s core ownership problem.

Keycloak provides the most control and uses standard protocols, including OIDC, OAuth 2.0 and SAML. [Keycloak capabilities](https://www.keycloak.org/) But production operation requires TLS, a production database, reverse proxying, health management and generally multiple clustered instances for availability. [Keycloak production guidance](https://www.keycloak.org/server/configuration-production) PetSpotR currently benefits far more from a managed identity service than from owning that infrastructure.

## Recommended authorization model

I would implement these boundaries:

- Normalize every authenticated user to an internal principal keyed by `issuer + subject`; never use email as the ownership key.
- Record report ownership privately when the report is created.
- Allow contact email to differ from account email, but never let that change ownership.
- Keep `reporter`, `finder`, `shelter member` and `operator` permissions in PetSpotR.
- Use Identity Platform custom claims only for coarse, server-assigned roles such as `operator`.
- Never put identity tokens, emails or provider-specific user objects into Pub/Sub events.
- Use secure, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite` session cookies with CSRF protection and recent-authentication checks for sensitive operations.
- Return consistent `401`, `403`, and ownership-hiding `404` responses.
- Record successful and rejected privileged actions in an audit collection.
- Put the provider behind a small Go `Authenticator` interface so switching providers does not rewrite every handler.

The best first shippable slice would be: **Identity Platform configuration, Auth emulator support, provider-neutral Go authentication middleware, and browser login/session/logout—with no status mutation yet.** The following slice can attach authenticated ownership to newly created reports, after which the lifecycle endpoints can safely be exposed.

No repository files were changed during this assessment.

+
+### Human Identity Sessions
+
+The web frontend has a provider-neutral human session boundary backed by
+Google Identity Platform through the Firebase Admin Go SDK. It is deployed
+consumer-first and defaults to `disabled`, including on Cloud Run, until the
+later infrastructure and sign-in UI slices activate it. Existing report and
+demo routes do not use the session yet, and pet lifecycle mutation routes
+remain unexposed.
+
+| `PETSPOTR_IDENTITY_MODE` | Required configuration | Cookie policy |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `disabled` or unset | None | Session routes return `404 Not Found` |
+| `local-emulator` | `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`, `FIREBASE_AUTH_EMULATOR_HOST` without an `http://` scheme | Local HTTP cookie names without `Secure` |
+| `gcp` | Application Default Credentials; optional explicit `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` | `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict`, host-only cookies |
+
+`POST /api/v1/session` exchanges a recently issued, verified-email Identity
+Platform ID token for a five-day server session. `GET /api/v1/session` verifies
+the cookie signature, expiry, user state, and revocation before returning the
+normalized issuer, subject, email, and sign-in provider. `DELETE
+/api/v1/session` clears the browser session. Login and logout require the
+double-submit token returned by `GET /api/v1/session/csrf`; provider tokens and
+session cookies are never returned in JSON.
+
+Start the pinned Authentication emulator from one terminal:
+
+```bash
+mise x node@24 -- npx --yes firebase-tools@15.25.1 \
+  emulators:start --only auth --project demo-petspotr-auth
+```
+
+Then run the real ID-token-to-session journey from another terminal:
+
+```bash
+FIREBASE_AUTH_EMULATOR_HOST=127.0.0.1:9099 \
+GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.5 \
+  go test ./e2e -count=1 -v \
+  -run '^TestIdentityPlatformSessionJourneyWithAuthEmulator$'
+```
+
+The contract creates a verified emulator user, obtains an emulator-issued ID
+token, exercises CSRF rejection, establishes and verifies the session through
+the real web server, logs out, and confirms the session no longer authenticates.
+Use the `demo-` project exactly as shown so an accidentally missing emulator
+cannot reach a billable Firebase project.
